Hi Alex / Priya —

Thanks again for your time today. Quick recap from our discovery so we’re aligned and I can loop in our infra/solutions team for an architecture call: 

Goals / non-functional targets you mentioned:
- Time-to-first-token (TTFT): target <= 120ms P95 at peak load (you mentioned 50 concurrent streaming sessions)
- Sustained throughput: ~200 req/s for the traffic window; short bursts up to 400 req/s
- Concurrency: typical per-region concurrent streams ~50, occasional spikes to 100
- Streaming: SSE preferred (server-sent events) for browser clients; WebSocket fallback needed for mobile/web-socket-heavy clients
- Chunk cadence: prefer chunk flush every 200–300ms (aim for smooth UX), but can tolerate up to 500ms in some flows

Ask items I promised to follow up on:
1) We’ll send a short perf / TTFT datasheet and an example payload so you can validate locally (attached).
2) Can you share: a) a representative request payload (size in tokens / bytes), b) expected average output length (tokens), and c) an example traffic profile (rps over time)?
3) Any security/compliance must-haves (SOC 2, IP residency) — I’ve attached the security questionnaire you mentioned for your convenience.

Next step: Marissa (solutions) is looping in to answer a couple of technical questions on how TTFT is measured and how streaming chunk cadence is controlled. After that we’ll schedule a 45-min architecture / perf call.

Thanks —

Thanks Aditya — good summary. A few clarification Qs from our side before the architecture call: 

1) When you say TTFT, is that measured from when the request reaches Redwood’s edge/load balancer, or from the client sending the request? We want to be sure auth / CDN / TLS handshake implications are accounted for in our SLA calculations.

2) For streaming chunk cadence: can Redwood guarantee maximum inter-chunk latency (e.g., never more than 500ms between chunks) under load? Also, can you control chunk size vs cadence (e.g., flush every N tokens or every X ms)?

3) Under batching (to improve throughput), what are the knobs to keep TTFT low for VIP traffic? Is there a way to reserve capacity / reserved concurrency for critical streams?

4) Do you have a perf test plan / harness we can run against a staging endpoint (we’re happy to run tests on our side)?

Attached our filled security questionnaire (see edgeai_security_questionnaire.xlsx).

From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
To: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@edgeai.com>, Priya Singh <priya.singh@edgeai.com>

Subject: Re: TTFT + streaming requirements — post-call recap & next steps

Hi Alex / Priya —

Thanks for the great questions — I’ll answer each directly and add practical guidance you can use for testing: 

1) TTFT definition and measurement:
- At Redwood we define TTFT as: server-side time from when the request is received by the inference front-door (post-auth and routing) to the moment the first token byte is returned to the client. That means network TLS handshake / client -> edge egress time is outside the server-side TTFT number; for an end-to-end SLA you should add the client->edge RTT and any CDN overhead.
- Typical numbers on our Dedicated pools (small-medium model, optimized kernel): P50 ~ 50–70ms, P95 ~ 90–150ms (depends on sequence length and batch behavior). We can hit the sub-120ms P95 target with reserved capacity and low-latency tuning.

2) Streaming (SSE vs WebSocket) and chunk cadence:
- We support both SSE and WebSocket streaming. SSE is straightforward for browser-based clients; WebSocket is fully supported as a persistent socket with identical token-stream semantics.
- Chunk cadence control: we expose two mechanisms: time-based flush (flush every X ms) and token-count flush (flush every N tokens). Defaults are 200–300ms cadence or flush after 16 tokens, whichever comes first. These are configurable per-route.
- Inter-chunk guarantees: under normal operating conditions with reserved capacity we maintain inter-chunk latencies under 300ms at target concurrency. We can advertise a 500ms max inter-chunk bound in SLA language for reserved pools; for best-effort shared capacity max inter-chunk latency may be higher during large bursts.

3) Batching, reserved concurrency and low-latency mode:
- Batching improves throughput but can increase TTFT when the system aggregates requests to fill a batch. To mitigate this for critical traffic we provide:
  * Reserved concurrency / reserved capacity (guaranteed slots on the GPU pool).
  * Low-latency mode: a per-route config that limits aggregation delay (max_wait_ms) and reduces max_batch_size. In practice we set max_wait_ms=10–20ms for sub-120ms TTFT targets.
  * Priority routing: VIP traffic can bypass large-batch queues and go to a low-latency execution pool.

4) Perf test plan / harness:
- We have a perf harness and recommended test plan (included in performance_harness_instructions.md). High level:
  * Run a baseline single-client streaming test with representative payload (attached example_payload.json) at target token sizes.
  * Ramp to target concurrency (50), then sustained throughput (200 req/s), record TTFT P50/P95/P99 and inter-chunk latency distribution.
  * Run tests with low-latency mode on vs off to measure impact of batching.

Practical guidance for your inputs to us:
- Send one representative request payload (JSON) and an average/99th percentile output length in tokens.
- If you have a traffic timeline (rps vs time) we can model cost and suggest instance sizing.

I’ll attach a short TTFT datasheet and the harness instructions to this thread; Aditya will coordinate a 45-min architecture call for next week.

Thanks —
Marissa Cole
